analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 5% minimum tax on corporations importing goods at inflated prices to shift profits abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote, and died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Some multinational corporations pay their overseas affiliates artificially high prices for goods they import into the US. Those inflated payments reduce the corporation's reported American income, so it pays less US tax. This bill would impose an alternative minimum tax of 5% on the US sales receipts of any large importer (over $10 million in sales and over $10 million in imports) that ends up owing less tax under the regular rules than under this 5% floor, ensuring such companies pay at least that minimum.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers in general, since companies that shift profits out of the country through inflated import pricing would no longer be able to drive their US tax bill toward zero; the minimum tax guarantees them at least 5% of US receipts. Domestic manufacturers who compete against imports also gain somewhat, because their rivals could no longer gain both a tax advantage and a pricing scheme at the same time.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes an alternative minimum tax equal to 5% of a covered corporation's net business receipts in the US, so the company cannot reduce its tax below that floor no matter how its import prices are arranged.

It applies to any corporation, foreign or domestic, with over $10 million in US sales of its manufactured products and over $10 million of imports by it or affiliates it controls (5% ownership or board control), closing the route of shifting income through a subsidiary.
The tax applies only when this minimum exceeds what the corporation owes under all other sections of the tax code, so companies paying taxes honestly under the regular rules are untouched.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations that import parts or products into the US at inflated prices from affiliates they control — the bill's stated targets. If those costs are passed along, US consumers could see somewhat higher prices on imported goods; importers using honest pricing are not covered.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinational importers pricing through foreign affiliates

drawbacks.text: A 5% tax on sales receipts is a tax on revenue, not profit, so it could hit low-margin importers hard even when their US operations are barely profitable, and those costs may be passed to consumers in prices.
Determining whether import prices are 'artificially inflated' is a difficult valuation question, and the bill taxes receipts regardless of whether the price distortion is proven for a given year.
A US-only minimum tax on importers could invite retaliation or trade disputes with trading partners, since it effectively raises the cost of importing relative to domestic production.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea — making large importers pay at least a minimum tax when inflated related-party pricing erodes their US tax base — addresses a real fairness problem. But a flat 5% receipts tax is a blunt instrument: it taxes struggling importers the same as profit-shifters and does not distinguish proven manipulation from ordinary pricing. A better-designed version would target the pricing distortion itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on its first day, got no cosponsors, no hearing, no vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Kanjorski introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax legislation.
No other action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote appears in the bill's action history.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its two-year life.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational importers that price goods through foreign affiliates keep paying no minimum floor on US taxes; no revenue was raised from profit-shifting.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan lineup can be read from the record.

industries.industry: Multinational importers with foreign manufacturing affiliates
industries.note: Companies importing more than $10 million of goods from controlled affiliates would owe at least 5% of US receipts, cutting off the tax benefit of inflated related-party prices. Their interest in avoiding this runs directly against taxpayers who otherwise absorb the lost revenue.

industries.industry: Foreign corporations selling manufactured goods in the US
industries.note: The bill explicitly covers foreign corporations meeting the sales and import thresholds, so foreign-based manufacturers could no longer report minimal US income via transfer pricing.
Importers' tax avoidance advantage would shrink, modestly leveling the field for US-based producers who pay tax on their full US income.
